unit.title: Establish and maintain community, government and business partnerships

summary: This unit teaches you to establish and maintain partnerships between a public or community body, government agencies and local businesses: finding and understanding partners, entering a community with respect, agreeing shared goals and roles, staying neutral and ethical, communicating and including everyone, managing disagreements, and reviewing and sustaining partnerships over time. It is written for supervisors and managers in Jamaican municipal corporations, agencies, ministries and community organisations.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. It prepares you to build and look after **partnerships**: agreed ways of working in which a community group, a government body and a business each contribute something and share in the results. Public managers in Jamaica rarely solve a local problem alone. A municipal corporation, a ministry's regional office or an agency needs the knowledge of residents, the authority and funds of government, and the skills, jobs and money of local firms.

At Level 5 you are the person who **starts the conversation, holds the partners together and keeps the trust**. You are not only a speaker at meetings: you map who matters, plan how to approach each partner, agree who does what, deal with politics and gifts properly, handle disagreements, and report honestly on results.
**Who it is for:** supervisors, officers and managers in public bodies, non-governmental organisations (NGOs), community-based organisations (CBOs) and businesses that work with the public sector.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in practice
rows: Understand why partnerships matter and what each sector offers
Explain what community, government and business partners want and can give, and why working across sectors gets results none of them can reach alone.
Find and map partners
List the groups, agencies and firms with a stake in an issue, map their interest and influence, and record the community's own assets.
Enter a community and approach partners properly
Listen first, work through recognised leaders and official channels, and make each approach fit the partner.
Agree shared goals, roles and resources
Run a joint planning meeting, agree aims, roles, measures and a written agreement, and track what each partner puts in.
Stay neutral and ethical
Keep politics out, handle gifts, sponsorship, conflicts of interest and personal data correctly, and refuse to be used for private lobbying.
Communicate, build trust and include everyone
Choose the right channels, report back in plain language, give weaker partners a real voice, and keep your promises.
Maintain relationships and manage conflict
Keep a partner register, follow an engagement plan, hand over contacts when staff move, and resolve disputes by looking at interests.
Review, report and sustain
Measure results and relationships, report honestly, and plan so that the benefits last after the agency's funding ends.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** with scenario questions and short sums on resources and percentages.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms such as CBO, CSR, social capital) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Group practical tasks**: a partner map with a one-year engagement plan and two neutral letters, and a facilitated partners' forum with a follow-up letter and a feedback survey. Each member has a named role.

blocks.note: Check every percentage and ratio twice, by two routes. A partnership report with a wrong figure loses the partners' trust quickly.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Why partnerships, and what each sector brings

blocks.p: A **partnership** is a working relationship in which two or more organisations agree to pursue a shared aim, contribute resources and share risks and results. It is more than a one-off favour or a contract to buy something. Complex local problems such as youth unemployment, a run-down market, flooding, crime or school drop-out have many causes. No single body holds all the answers, money or reach.

head: Sector
Typical partners
What they usually want
What they usually bring
Common limits
rows: Community
Citizens' associations, community development committees, churches, youth clubs, farmers' groups, cooperatives, parent-teacher associations, community-based organisations (CBOs)
A better life in their area: safety, jobs, services, respect and a say in decisions
Local knowledge and trust
Volunteers and time
Access to residents
Ideas that fit the place
Little money, volunteers' limited time, and past disappointments with outsiders
Government
Ministries, agencies, municipal corporations, the Social Development Commission (SDC), schools, health centres, the police
To meet their mandate and targets, use public money well and answer to the public
Authority and legal powers
Public funds and programmes
Technical staff
Data and planning links
Rules, budgets set a year ahead, slow approvals and staff transfers
Business
Shops, hotels, manufacturers, farms, banks, business associations, chambers of commerce
Customers, a skilled workforce, a good name and a stable local market
Cash and goods (in-kind support)
Jobs, training places and work experience
Management skills
Equipment and transport
Profit pressure, short planning horizons, and concern about favouritism or reputation

blocks.p: **Non-governmental organisations (NGOs)** are non-profit bodies independent of government, such as charities. They often act as a bridge, bringing expertise and links to funders.

ul: **Resources and reach:** each sector holds what the others lack, so together they cover the whole problem.
**Fit:** projects designed with residents match real needs and are more likely to be used and protected.
**Joined-up effort:** agencies stop duplicating each other and residents stop getting mixed messages.
**Shared risk and shared credit:** a failure or a success belongs to all, which keeps partners committed.

blocks.p: Partnerships are not a way to **hand your duties to someone else**. A public body stays responsible for its legal and public duties. It also does not replace a budget: partners add to, not substitute for, public funding.

terms: Corporate social responsibility (CSR)
The way a business takes responsibility for its effect on society and supports community causes.
Goodwill
The good reputation and trust a business or body gains when it is seen to help the community.
Social capital
The networks, trust and shared norms in a community that help people work together.
In-kind support
Help given as goods, services, staff time or use of space rather than cash.
Collective impact
Organisations from different sectors agreeing a common agenda, shared measures and joint activities to solve a complex problem.

blocks.note: In Jamaica, the Social Development Commission (SDC) works with communities across the island, and Parish Development Committees (PDCs) bring community, government and business together to plan local development in each parish. Municipal corporations (the municipal corporations, renamed in 2016) are a key local partner. Start by finding out which of these already operate where you work.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Preparing: understanding the community and mapping partners

blocks.p: Good partnerships start with homework. Before you send a letter or call a meeting, find out about the **issue**, the **place** and the **people**. Many partnerships fail because an outsider arrived with a ready-made plan.

blocks.h: Entering a community with no contacts

flow: Read the data on the issue (clinic, school, police, municipal and census figures)
Talk to people who know the area: community officers, SDC staff, the police community liaison, teachers, church leaders
Meet recognised local leaders and groups and listen first; ask who else should be involved
Explain who you are, what your body can and cannot do, and what you are exploring
Visit again, attend local events, and only then propose joint work

blocks.p: The first visit is for **listening**. Do not arrive with a press launch, a list of promises, or an outside firm to run the project. If you promise what you cannot deliver, you will not be trusted a second time.

**Asset mapping** means finding the skills, groups, places and resources a community already has. Assets include a carpenter who trains boys, a church hall, a women's group that runs a lunch programme, a retired teacher, a football club, a clinic. Starting from assets, not only problems, shows respect, builds on strengths and lowers the cost of the project. A community with assets is a **partner**, not only a beneficiary.

A **stakeholder** is any person, group or organisation affected by an issue or able to influence it. List them in three columns: community, government and business. For each, note what it **wants**, what it can **give**, its **mandate** (for a public body, what the law lets it do) and the right **contact**.
A common planning tool sorts partners by how much **power** (influence) they hold and how much **interest** they have in the issue.

head: Power
Low interest
High interest
rows: High power
**Keep satisfied.**
Brief them regularly and consult before big decisions. Example: a large employer or senior officer who is not yet involved.
**Manage closely.**
Core partners: involve them in decisions and meet often. Example: the agency, the main business partner, the community committee.
Low power
**Monitor.**
Keep informed through general channels. Example: distant firms and groups.
**Keep informed and involve.**
Often the people most affected, such as vendors, fishers or residents. Make sure their voice is heard, because their low power is a risk to the project if ignored.

blocks.note: Never read a position in the grid as a measure of someone's worth. A small group of fishers has low formal power but holds the knowledge that decides whether a fishing-beach project works.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: Understanding each partner before you approach

ul: What does it want to **gain** and what can it **contribute**?
What are its rules, timetable and decision-makers?
Has it worked with the public body before, and how did it go?
Are there any conflicts of interest (for example, does the business have a licence or tender pending with your body)?

blocks.p: Record all of this in a **partner register** (a simple spreadsheet or file): name, sector, contact, interests, contribution, history and next contact date.

blocks.note: A **chamber of commerce or business association** can be the most efficient route to many small firms at once. Use community development committees and citizens' associations in the same way for residents.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Building the partnership: approaching partners, agreeing goals and roles

head: Partner
What works
What to avoid
rows: Community group
Meet at a time and place that suits them
Plain language, no jargon
Show how residents will help decide, not only attend
Respect local leadership and traditions
Surprising them with a finished plan
Dealing only with the loudest voice
Visits only at election time
Government body
Use the **proper official channel**: a formal letter or meeting request to the head or the right officer
Know its mandate and what it can legally do
Link to existing plans, such as the parish's local sustainable development plan
Going around the chain of command
Asking a body to do what the law does not allow
Duplicating its programme
Business
Show the business case: **goodwill, local trust, a skilled workforce, a stronger local market**
Offer a clear, small first request
Find an internal **champion** who promotes the partnership inside the firm and keeps it moving
Credit it publicly and fairly
Appealing only to guilt
Asking for open-ended funding
Promising favours in licensing or tenders

flow: Hold a facilitated meeting where every partner states its concerns and what it can offer
Agree the **shared goal** in one sentence
Agree what each partner will do, with who, by when, and with what resources
Agree a small set of **shared measures** (for example young people placed in jobs or training)
Write it down in an agreement and share it with everyone

blocks.p: The first thing to agree is the **shared goal and each partner's role**. Without it, partners work at cross purposes. A small set of shared measures lets everyone see joint progress, instead of each partner counting only its own activity.
Even a simple partnership needs a written record, often called a **memorandum of understanding (MOU)** or partnership agreement. It is not always a legal contract. It normally records:

ul: the purpose and shared goal
each partner's role, resources and responsibilities
who leads, how decisions are made and how often partners meet
how money, goods and credit will be handled and accounted for
how information, including personal data, will be shared and protected
how problems will be raised and settled
how long the agreement runs, how it will be reviewed and how a partner can leave

blocks.note: A partnership with a government body may need formal approval, or legal advice, before you commit public money or sign anything. Check your own organisation's rules first.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Public bodies like to show that their money **attracted** other resources. Count cash and in-kind support, and put a fair value on volunteer time.

**Partners added per J$1 of public money = partners' total contribution ÷ agency's contribution.** Example: an agency puts in J$4 million. Business partners add J$6 million in cash and J$2 million in goods, and volunteers' time is valued at J$1 million. Partners' total = J$9 million. Partners added J$9 million ÷ J$4 million = **J$2.25** for every J$1 from the agency. The total programme is J$13 million, so the agency's share is 4 ÷ 13 = about 31%.

blocks.note: Always say how in-kind and volunteer time were valued, and keep the evidence. An unsupported figure damages credibility.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: When many small groups are involved, work through **umbrella bodies**: a business association, a federation of cooperatives, a community development committee. For Jamaicans living overseas who want to help their parish, use **diaspora associations** and online meetings.

A public body that works with communities, firms and politicians must be, and be seen to be, **fair and politically neutral**. Trust is the main asset of a partnership. One careless act can destroy it.

head: Situation
What to do
Why
rows: An elected representative wants to launch the partnership at a party rally
Politely decline the party event and offer a non-party, official event open to all
The public body serves everyone and must not be seen to favour a party
A business offers to sponsor your event if its logo appears on your licence application forms
Decline that condition. Offer logo recognition at the event only if the sponsorship policy allows it
It could suggest that the firm will be favoured when licences are decided
A partner sends an expensive gift at year end
Follow the organisation's **gifts policy**: declare it, and return it or hand it to the organisation if it is not permitted
Gifts can create an obligation or the appearance of one
A business asks to use the partnership to lobby government for a tax break
Decline: it is outside the partnership's purpose and the public body cannot take sides in private interest
The partnership has an agreed public goal, not a private one
Several firms want to sponsor a programme
Use **clear, fair criteria** (fit with aims, no conflict, ability to deliver), apply them to all and record the decision
Fair, open choices protect the body from claims of favouritism
You are asked to share residents' names and health needs between partners
First check against the **data protection law**: share only what is needed, for the agreed purpose, with consent where required, held securely
Personal data belongs to the person; misuse harms residents and the body

blocks.p: A **conflict of interest** exists when a person's private interest (a relative's business, a personal friendship, a financial gain) could affect, or look as if it could affect, their official judgement. The rule is: **declare it, record it, and step out of the decision**. Public bodies also follow **procurement rules**: when the body buys goods or services, including from a partner, the process must be open, fair, recorded and give value for money.

blocks.note: In public service, how a decision looks matters almost as much as how it is made. If you would be uncomfortable seeing it on the evening news, change it or declare it.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Some communities, for example Maroon communities in Jamaica, have their own leadership and traditions. Learn about them, respect them and work through them. Do not assume that one leader speaks for everyone. Do not photograph or publish residents' stories without their consent.

ul: Follow **employment law** for staff and paid helpers, and keep volunteers safe.
Follow the **data protection law** for personal information.
Follow **procurement rules for public bodies** when buying.
Keep accounts of any money handled and give receipts.

blocks.p: Refer to the policies of your own organisation for the detail. This unit asks you to know the **purpose** of these rules, not their section numbers.

Trust is built less by what you say than by **doing what you said you would do, on time**. Other actions that build credibility: being honest about limits, admitting mistakes, listening, sharing information early, giving credit, and not appearing only when you need something.

blocks.note: A community leader who says an agency 'only comes around at election time' is giving you useful feedback. Meet the leader, listen, and agree regular contact. Do not argue on the radio.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Audience
Suitable channels
rows: Elderly or rural residents with little internet
Community meetings, church announcements, notice boards, flyers, local radio, home visits
Young people
Social media, WhatsApp groups, youth clubs, schools, short messages
Government partners
Formal letters, e-mail to named officers, scheduled meetings, written progress reports
Business partners
Short, results-based updates, briefings at business association meetings, events where they are thanked
Everyone, at the end of a stage
A **town hall** or public meeting, plain-language report, local media

blocks.p: Report back **in plain language, through local meetings and media**, on what the partnership has achieved, what it has not, and what happens next. Use local languages where helpful. Avoid acronyms residents do not know.

blocks.h: Community participation: how much real say?

head: Level
What it looks like
rows: Informing
You tell residents what you decided.
Consulting
You ask for views but decide yourself.
Involving and collaborating
Residents help set priorities and take part in decisions.
Empowering
Residents lead and the agency supports.

blocks.p: The approach that gives a community the most real say is **involving residents in setting priorities and in decisions**. Publicly thanking and crediting partners shows respect and encourages continued support.
When a large hotel group or ministry sits with a small cooperative of fishers or vendors, the small group may say little. That weakens trust and the quality of decisions. The convenor can:

ul: hold some meetings where the small group works or lives, at times that suit them
use **smaller sessions**, so quieter people can speak
give each partner equal speaking time and a say in the agenda
provide transport, childcare, or a small stipend where possible
support small groups with training, and pay or credit their contribution fairly
use plain language and a facilitator who is not tied to any partner

blocks.p: **Networking** also matters. Attend parish development committee meetings and business forums even when no project is running. You build contacts and learn local priorities, so that when a need arises you already know whom to call.
A partnership that goes quiet after the launch is losing trust. To **maintain** it:

ul: keep **regular contact**, share progress and ask for views
keep a **partner register** so contacts, interests, commitments and history are not stored in one officer's head
use a yearly **engagement plan**: priority partners, aims, contact methods, frequency, owners and timing
invite partners to events, thank and credit them
change plans only after talking to those affected
keep your promises on dates and money

blocks.p: Partnerships built on one person's relationships can collapse when that person moves. The manager should arrange **handover meetings**, introduce the new officer to each partner in person, and update the contact records.

flow: Raise it early and in private, with facts
Ask what has changed and what support is needed
Agree clear steps, dates and a follow-up date
Record the agreement
If the failure continues, review that partner's role openly, and agree a change, rather than ignoring it or blaming it in public

blocks.p: Disagreements are normal, especially when interests differ: a business wants trading hours and customers; residents want sleep and safety. Act early, before positions harden or the dispute reaches the media.

flow: Meet each side separately and listen to understand its **interests** (what it needs and why), not only its position (what it demands)
Check the facts and gather the data
Bring them together, with ground rules and a neutral facilitator
List the interests, generate several options, and test each against all interests
Agree actions with owners and dates, record them and review later

head: Position
Possible underlying interests
Possible option
rows: 'Close the venue by 10 p.m.'
Residents: sleep, safety for children
Soundproofing, a noise limit, a complaints line
'We need to open until 2 a.m.'
Owner: income, staff jobs
Later hours on weekends only, with agreed noise controls and a review in three months

blocks.note: If you take sides in a dispute between partners, you stop being a convenor. Stay fair, and keep to the agreed purpose of the partnership.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: Risks of depending on one partner

blocks.p: If a community feeding programme gets all its food from one supermarket, it may stop if that supermarket withdraws. Spread the risk: several suppliers, a back-up plan and a reserve.
A review has two parts: **results** and **relationships**.

head: Part
Examples of measures
rows: Results (outcomes)
Jobs or training places gained, households reached, drop in dumping, school attendance, changes in participants' skills or incomes
Outputs (activity)
Workshops held, meetings, leaflets, people attending
Resources
Partners' cash and in-kind support for each J$1 of public money; cost per participant
Relationships
Partner satisfaction, trust, attendance at meetings, speed of decisions, number of problems raised and settled

blocks.p: **Outputs** show what you did; **outcomes** show what changed. A report that says only '40 workshops were held' does not show value. Add the changes in participants' jobs, skills or incomes.

ul: **Percentage** = part ÷ whole × 100. If 33 of 44 partners rate the relationship good or very good, that is 33 ÷ 44 = 0.75, so **75%**.
**Percentage change** = (new − old) ÷ old × 100. If forum attendance falls from 80 to 68, the change is −12 ÷ 80 = **15% fall**. If it rises from 25 to 40, the change is 15 ÷ 25 = 60% rise.
**Partners added per J$1** = partners' contribution ÷ agency's contribution (see earlier).
**Cost per participant** = total cost ÷ number of participants.

blocks.note: Work every sum twice, by two routes. For example, check a 15% fall by working out 15% of 80 (12) and subtracting from 80 (68).
blocks.label: Tip

flow: Collect results data against the agreed shared measures
Ask partners how they feel about the relationship, using a short regular survey of 6 to 8 questions on communication, trust, fairness and results
Hold a review meeting with all partners to look at results and views together
Agree what to continue, change or end
Report in plain language to partners, the community and the public body's management

blocks.p: If a partnership has produced little after several years, **review results and views together, then agree next steps**: strengthen it, change its focus, reduce it or end it with thanks. Do not simply let it fade.

blocks.h: Sustaining the partnership after funding ends

blocks.p: Plan for sustainability from the start, not in the last months. A partnership survives after the agency's funding ends when:

ul: **local people and groups have the skills to lead it**: training in planning, finance, record keeping and running meetings
the activities that matter most have been agreed and costed
there are several sources of support, not one
partners have taken on roles, for example a business adopting the programme as part of its CSR
the partnership is linked to local plans, such as the parish development plan
records and contacts are passed on in good order

blocks.note: When funding ends, thank partners publicly, report results, and tell people clearly what will and will not continue. A tidy ending protects your reputation for the next partnership.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: explain why a public body works with community, government and business partners together
describe what each sector wants and brings
enter a new community by listening first, working through recognised leaders and mapping assets
map stakeholders and place them on a power and interest grid
approach a government body through official channels, and a business with a clear business case
run a joint planning meeting and agree shared goals, roles and measures in a written agreement
calculate partners' contributions, percentages, percentage changes and cost per participant
stay politically neutral and handle gifts, sponsorship, conflicts of interest and personal data correctly
choose communication channels to suit each audience and report back in plain language
make a partnership more inclusive when partners have unequal power
keep a partner register and engagement plan, and hand over relationships when staff move
handle a disagreement by exploring interests, and a non-performing partner by open discussion
review a partnership on results and relationships, and plan for it to continue after funding ends

terms: Partnership
An agreed way of working in which partners contribute resources and share risks and results.
Stakeholder
Anyone affected by an issue or able to influence it.
CBO / NGO
Community-based organisation (such as a youth club); non-governmental organisation (a non-profit independent of government).
Asset mapping
Finding the skills, groups and resources a community already has.
Power and interest grid
A tool that sorts partners by influence and interest to decide how to engage each.
Mandate
What a public body is legally allowed and required to do.
MOU
Memorandum of understanding: a written record of partners' aims and roles.
CSR / goodwill
A business's responsibility to society; the good name it gains by helping.
Social capital
Networks, trust and shared norms that help people work together.
Collective impact
Cross-sector partners with a common agenda and shared measures.
Conflict of interest
A private interest that could affect, or seem to affect, official judgement.
Partner register
The record of each partner's contacts, interests, commitments and history.
Outputs / outcomes
What you did; what changed as a result.
Sustainability
The ability to keep delivering benefits after the first funding ends.

c1.title: Falmouth market district
c1.text: The Trelawny municipal corporation wants to revive the Falmouth market district, which has fallen quiet. Interested parties include the vendors' association (about 90 members, mostly women with small stalls), a heritage agency, a hotel group that takes cruise visitors past the market, a business association of shopkeepers, and a church that runs a Saturday feeding programme nearby. The corporation's officer, Mrs Opal Grant, has not worked with any of them before.

c2.title: Savanna-la-Mar fishing beach
c2.text: A government agency wants to improve the Savanna-la-Mar fishing beach with a partnership of fishers, an agency, and local firms. The fishers' cooperative has 40 members and rarely speaks at large meetings. A local ice-and-cold-storage company offers to pay for a new landing shed, but it has a licence application waiting with the agency. A Member of Parliament asks to open the shed at a constituency party meeting, and at year end the company sends the officer, Mr Andre Bryan, a large gift hamper.

c3.title: Mandeville youth mentoring programme
c3.text: A two-year youth mentoring programme in Mandeville was funded by an agency (J$6,000,000), business partners (J$9,000,000 in cash and J$3,000,000 in goods), and volunteer mentors whose time was valued at J$2,000,000. It enrolled 400 young people, and 260 of them were placed in jobs, apprenticeships or training. In the partner review, 35 of the 50 partners rated the relationship good or very good. Attendance at the quarterly partners' forum fell from 80 to 68.

c4.title: Morant Bay water-harvesting project
c4.text: In a St Thomas community near Morant Bay, a partnership of the community development committee, a parish agency and a hardware firm installed water tanks. The firm has missed two delivery dates, and the committee chairman has complained publicly. The agency's funding ends in eighteen months. The project officer who built the partnership, Ms Janet Reid, is being transferred next month.

c5.title: Port Maria farmers' market link
c5.text: An agency in Port Maria is working with a farmers' group, a bank and a supermarket supplier on a scheme to get farmers' produce to market. Many farmers are over 55 and have little internet use. The bank wants to give residents a personal-finance workshop and asks the agency for the list of farmers with their phone numbers and loan balances held by another partner.

questions.q: Before approaching any of these groups, what should Mrs Grant first find out about each one?
o: How its officers voted at the last general election, so she can avoid anyone who might cause political trouble
What it wants to gain and can contribute
How quickly it could sign a funding agreement, so that the project can start in the current financial year
How many of its members live outside the parish, since they might be hard to reach for meetings
questions.why: A partner approach is only persuasive if it matches what the partner wants and can give. Interests and contributions come first; other facts follow.

questions.q: Mrs Grant places the vendors' association (many members, little formal power, very high interest in the outcome) on a power and interest grid. What should she do about it?
o: Keep it informed and involve it closely, because it is the group most affected
Monitor it through general notices only, because its formal power is low and larger partners will decide
Brief it after the plan is agreed with the hotel group, so the vendors only receive a finished proposal
Leave it to the shopkeepers' business association to speak for it, since that body has more influence
questions.why: Low power with high interest means involve and keep informed. Ignoring the people most affected is a major risk to the project.

questions.q: Mrs Grant wants help from a government agency that holds heritage-site records. How should she make the request?
o: Informally, by asking a friend who works there to pass over the records as a favour to the corporation
By asking the Member of Parliament for the area to instruct the agency to cooperate with the corporation
By inviting the agency's staff to a public market meeting and raising the request there in front of residents
Through a formal request to the agency's proper official channel, linked to its mandate
questions.why: Government bodies respond to formal requests that fit their mandate. Going around channels, or through a politician, can create problems of fairness and neutrality.

questions.q: Which argument is most likely to persuade the hotel group to join?
o: The group has a duty to repay the corporation for the licences and approvals it has received over the years
The corporation can offer the group first choice of vendors' stalls and the best market locations
A busier, safer market will improve the visitor experience and local goodwill
All large businesses in the parish are expected to contribute to council revival projects and the group should follow
questions.why: Business partners respond to a business case such as customers, goodwill and a stronger local market. Pressure or promised favours are poor and unethical grounds.

questions.q: The cooperative's members rarely speak in joint meetings with larger partners. What should the convenor do?
o: Ask the larger partners to speak for the fishers, to save time and keep the meeting focused on decisions
Keep the large meetings as they are and send the fishers the minutes afterwards for their comments
Meet them at the beach in smaller sessions, at times that suit the fishing day
Invite only the cooperative's chairman and treat his view as the view of all forty members
questions.why: Power imbalances are reduced by changing how meetings work. Meeting people where they work and in small groups lets quieter partners speak.

questions.q: The agency receives the cold-storage company's offer while its licence application is waiting. What is the best way to handle this?
o: Accept the offer at once, because a new landing shed benefits the whole fishing community and the beach
Declare the conflict, keep licensing separate from the offer, and apply the agency's sponsorship criteria to it
Tell the company that the licence will move faster if its offer is increased to cover more of the beach
Reject all offers from any firm that has ever dealt with the agency, whatever the criteria say
questions.why: A pending licence creates a conflict of interest. Declare it, separate the two decisions and apply fair criteria so the choice cannot look like a favour.

questions.q: How should the agency answer the Member of Parliament's request to open the shed at a party meeting?
o: Offer a non-party, official opening that is open to all residents and partners alike
Agree, because the MP represents the area and has asked politely for a public body's help with the opening
Agree, provided the party meeting is held on a weekend and no public money is spent on the event
Decline and keep the shed closed until the next election has passed and the political situation is calmer
questions.why: Public bodies must be, and be seen to be, politically neutral. A public, non-party event lets the MP take part without making the partnership partisan.

questions.q: What should Mr Bryan do with the large gift hamper?
o: Keep it for now, because the licence decision has not yet been made and nothing can be said to be owed
Share it among the office staff and say nothing, so that no single person benefits from the gift
Accept it and send the company a similar gift in return, to show that the agency is not in its debt
Follow the gifts policy: declare the hamper and then return it or hand it over as the policy directs
questions.why: A valuable gift from a firm with business before the body can create an obligation or the appearance of one. Declaring it and following the policy protects the officer and the agency.

questions.q: The programme officer reports the leverage ratio to the agency's board. Which statement of it is correct?
o: J$1.50, found by dividing the total programme of J$20,000,000 by the businesses' J$9,000,000 in cash and goods
J$3.33, found by dividing the total programme of J$20,000,000 by the agency's J$6,000,000
J$0.43, found by dividing the agency's J$6,000,000 by the partners' J$14,000,000
Partners added about J$2.33 of resources for each J$1 the agency spent
questions.why: Partners added J$9,000,000 + J$3,000,000 + J$2,000,000 = J$14,000,000. Divide by the agency's J$6,000,000 to get J$2.33. (Total programme J$20,000,000.)

questions.q: What was the agency's share of the total resources?
o: 43%, found by dividing the agency's J$6,000,000 by the partners' J$14,000,000
70%, found by dividing the partners' J$14,000,000 by the total of J$20,000,000
33%, found by dividing the agency's J$6,000,000 by the businesses' J$18,000,000
questions.why: The total was J$6M + J$9M + J$3M + J$2M = J$20M. Agency share is 6 ÷ 20 = 30%. A common slip is to divide by the partners' J$14M (43%).

questions.q: What is the cost per young person enrolled, using the total resources?
o: J$15,000, using only the agency's J$6,000,000 shared among the 400 young people enrolled
J$35,000, using only the J$14,000,000 added by partners shared among the 400 young people
J$77,000, using the total resources shared among the 260 young people placed in jobs or training
questions.why: J$20,000,000 ÷ 400 young people = J$50,000. Using only the agency's money (J$6M ÷ 400 = J$15,000) would hide the true cost.

questions.q: Attendance at the quarterly forum fell from 80 to 68. How should the manager read and use this?
o: As a 15% fall, so she should ask partners why attendance dropped and adjust the forum to suit them
As a 12% fall, which is small enough to leave until the next annual review of the partnership
As a 15% rise, because 68 is still a large number of people to have in one room at the same time
As a fall of 12 people, which needs no action while the partnership is still meeting its other targets
questions.why: (80 − 68) ÷ 80 = 15%. A fall in attendance is an early sign of declining engagement, so the manager should ask why and act, rather than assume success.

questions.q: The report says 400 young people enrolled and 260 were placed in jobs or training. Which statement best shows the programme's value?
o: 65% of the enrolled young people moved into work, an apprenticeship or training
400 young people were enrolled, which proves that the programme worked well for the whole parish
The programme held very many mentoring sessions, which shows how hard the partners and volunteers worked
The partners' cash contribution was large, which is the best sign that the programme gave good value
questions.why: 260 ÷ 400 = 65% placed. Outcomes (changes in people's jobs and skills) show value; outputs such as sessions and enrolments show only activity.

questions.q: The hardware firm has missed two delivery dates, and the chairman has criticised it publicly. What should Ms Reid do first?
o: Replace the firm immediately and announce the change at the next community meeting to calm the chairman
Say nothing further, because the firm is donating the tanks and should not be pressed on its timing
Ask the chairman to stop criticising the firm in public and take no other action until the tanks arrive
Discuss the delays privately with the firm, agree steps and dates, and record them
questions.why: Raise problems early and openly, in private, with facts. Agree clear steps and dates. If failure continues, review the role. Public blame or silence both damage the partnership.

questions.q: Ms Reid is transferred next month. What is the most important step to protect the partnership?
o: Leave a short note telling all the partners that the project will continue under new management
Ask the committee chairman to find out the new officer's name and contact details when they are posted
Hold handover meetings that introduce the new officer to each partner, and update the contact records
Keep running the partnership from her new post, by phone and e-mail, until the project ends
questions.why: Partnerships built on one person's relationships can fail when that person leaves. A proper handover, personal introductions and updated records keep trust.

questions.q: The agency's funding ends in eighteen months. Which preparation best helps the project survive?
o: Spend the remaining budget quickly on more tanks so that there is something visible to show the funders
Train committee members in planning, finance and record keeping so local people can lead it
Wait until the last three months before discussing with partners what should happen after the funding ends
Ask the hardware firm to take over all the costs and the whole responsibility for the project
questions.why: Sustainability depends on local people and groups having the skills to lead. Start early, agree what matters most, and spread support across several sources.

questions.q: Why should the agency not send the bank a list of farmers' names, phone numbers and loan balances?
o: Banks are not permitted by law to take part in any partnership that is led by a public agency
Personal data may be shared only for an agreed purpose, as the data protection law requires
Phone numbers change too often for a list to remain useful for more than a few weeks at a time
The farmers' group is the only body in the parish that is allowed to hold information about farmers
questions.why: The general aims of the data protection law are to collect and use only what is needed, for a stated purpose and with proper consent and security. Loan details are sensitive and sharing them could harm farmers.

questions.q: Many of the farmers are over 55 and rarely use the internet. What is the best way to keep them informed?
o: Community meetings, church announcements, printed flyers and local radio programmes
E-mail updates and regular posts on the agency's social media page, which are quick and cost almost nothing
A project website, with the link sent to the farmers' group chairman to pass on to members who ask
The bank's mobile banking app, because every farmer with an account can receive project news on it
questions.why: Channels must suit the audience. Face-to-face meetings, churches, printed flyers and radio reach people who are offline.

questions.q: Four weeks after the launch, the bank, the farmers' group and the agency each set their own targets for 'success'. What should be done?
o: Let each partner continue with its own targets and combine the three reports at the end of the year
Use the agency's measures only, because it is the public body and carries the legal responsibility
Delay measuring altogether until the scheme has run for a full year and results are more visible
Agree a small set of shared measures, so all partners can see joint progress towards one goal
questions.why: Partners who count different things cannot show joint progress. A shared goal and a few shared measures keep everyone working on the same result.

questions.q: A manager finds that her partnership with a business association has produced little after three years. What is the sound way to decide its future?
o: End the partnership at once, because three years is long enough for any partnership to show results
Continue unchanged, to avoid upsetting the association and its members, who still attend meetings
Review results and the partners' views together, then agree next steps
Ask the association to contribute more money, so that results improve over the next financial year
questions.why: A fair review looks at both results and relationships, with the partners, before choosing to strengthen, change or end a partnership. Letting it fade or ending it abruptly harms trust.
